impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that claims directed to using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering anti-CGRP antibody treatments. The case involves blockbuster migraine drugs (Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's competing product) and has major implications for the scope of patent protection available for antibody-based therapeutics defined by their functional properties.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biopharmaceutical companies claiming genus-level antibody patents, particularly where the specification discloses known methods for making and humanizing antibodies, supporting broader patent scope for biologic drug innovators.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader patent barriers when seeking to enter the anti-CGRP antibody market and analogous biologic drug markets, potentially delaying competition and increasing litigation risk.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model of expected function calls are directed to abstract ideas under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in allowing damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims were abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step-two analysis. The court also ruled that damages for foreign sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing territorial limits on patent damages. The decision impacts cybersecurity patents broadly.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing software and cybersecurity patents benefit from strengthened Alice eligibility scrutiny and the reinforcement of territorial limits on patent damages for foreign sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the cybersecurity and software space face heightened risk that claims directed to anomaly detection and similar computer-implemented methods will be invalidated as abstract under § 101.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis for the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether inventive contribution for patent inventorship can rest on ideas that are generally known.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict on trade secret misappropriation claims related to a cosmetic penile implant, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, holding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from the reinforced requirement that plaintiffs must demonstrate with specificity that claimed trade secrets are not generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher burden to prove protectability, and companies relying on trade secret claims as a competitive tool must ensure robust evidence that the information is truly secret and not generally known in the field.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit alleging that EOFlow misappropriated trade secrets related to insulin patch pump technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict in favor of Insulet, holding that the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The case involved former employees who allegedly shared CAD files and proprietary design information with a competitor developing a rival insulin pump.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's statute of limitations, providing a definitive defense against stale claims even where evidence of misappropriation may exist.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation; delays in filing suit risk permanent loss of DTSA remedies regardless of the strength of the underlying claim.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data via relay devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming-data patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas, but vacated the district court's refusal to find the case exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorneys' fees. The decision reinforces that data collection and processing claims in agricultural technology face significant § 101 hurdles.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech companies defending against patent assertions benefit from continued rigorous application of § 101 to data-collection claims, and the remand on exceptionality signals that defendants may recover fees when patentees assert clearly ineligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking patent protection for precision agriculture and IoT-based farming systems face heightened risk of invalidity under § 101, potentially diminishing the value of their patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement of multicore processor patents based on extraterritoriality and rejection of doctrine-of-equivalents theories, and whether the court properly struck damages expert theories for inadequate disclosure.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part Intel's summary judgment victory on VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding that the district court erred on at least one of its noninfringement grounds, and remanded for further proceedings. The decision addresses important issues regarding extraterritorial reach of U.S. patent law and discovery sanctions for damages theories.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against multinational semiconductor and technology companies benefit from the court's rejection of overly broad extraterritoriality defenses that could shield global product lines from U.S. infringement liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major technology companies like Intel face continued exposure to high-value patent infringement claims, and the decision limits the effectiveness of extraterritoriality as a complete defense to patent assertions involving globally distributed products.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court's damages analysis and infringement findings were proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the eligibility finding for some claims while affirming it for others, creating a split outcome across the asserted patent family involving communication standard technology. The court affirmed infringement and damages findings, upholding a jury verdict against LG. The decision is significant for standard-essential patent litigation in the broadcast and telecommunications industries.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to communications standards benefit from the affirmance of infringement and damages findings, and the partial affirmance of eligibility provides a roadmap for drafting claims that survive § 101 scrutiny.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face ongoing patent infringement liability, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the scope of protection for standard-related innovations.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish Article III standing even after granting an exclusive license, so long as the retained right to sue is not rendered illusory. This clarifies standing rules for patent owners who license extensively but retain enforcement rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners and licensing entities benefit from clarity that retaining the right to sue third parties, combined with other exclusionary rights, is sufficient for constitutional standing even after granting exclusive licenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potentially dispositive standing defense; the decision makes it harder to challenge a patent holder's right to sue based on the existence of an exclusive licensing arrangement.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge, and whether the on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that sales expressly disclose a prior art device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating engine controller reprogramming patents under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible regardless of the designee's personal knowledge and rejecting the argument that the on-sale bar requires express disclosure of functionality. The decision has broad implications for patent invalidity defenses based on prior commercial sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded use of 30(b)(6) corporate testimony in invalidity challenges and a broad interpretation of the on-sale bar that does not require public disclosure of the sold device's internal functionality.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges, as prior commercial sales of products need not have publicly disclosed the patented functionality to trigger the statutory bar.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's patents on wearable pulse oximetry devices.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement technology, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing models. The decision has significant implications for the wearable health technology industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device patent holders benefit from the affirmance of ITC exclusion orders as an effective enforcement mechanism against major technology companies importing infringing health-monitoring products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies incorporating health-monitoring features into consumer devices face significant import ban risk from ITC proceedings, potentially forcing costly redesigns or licensing negotiations with medical device patent holders.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) may obtain such a stay by voluntarily dismissing and refiling its declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling the action. The case arose from a pharmaceutical patent dispute between BioMarin and Ascendis over treatments for achondroplasia, where BioMarin sought to delay Ascendis's declaratory judgment of non-infringement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Declaratory judgment plaintiffs benefit from certainty that opponents cannot manipulate mandatory stay provisions through tactical refiling, preserving the ability to pursue timely resolution of patent disputes in district court.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the statutory deadline for requesting a mandatory stay of parallel district court litigation lose that procedural tool permanently, even through creative refiling strategies.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding a patent holder's damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent infringement case against Microsoft's Azure platform, vacating the summary judgment that had been premised on the absence of any damages proof. The decision emphasizes that district courts must carefully apply Daubert standards and should not effectively dispose of patent cases by excluding damages evidence without adequate justification.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's admonition that district courts should not use overly aggressive damages-expert exclusions to effectively grant summary judgment, preserving the right to trial on damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology companies defending patent suits face reduced ability to obtain dispositive rulings through Daubert challenges to damages experts, potentially increasing the cost and duration of patent litigation.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action challenging excessive PACER fees, upholding the settlement terms, attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives. The decision validates class actions challenging government fee practices and confirms the propriety of service awards to organizational class representatives.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users and confirms that class action mechanisms can effectively challenge excessive government fees, benefiting businesses and law firms that regularly use court electronic filing systems.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion could assert infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that Mylan's generic epoprostenol product did not infringe Actelion's patents, holding that the pH limitation must be measured at a field-standard temperature and that Actelion was barred from asserting doctrine-of-equivalents infringement. The decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent claim construction involving measurable physical parameters.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers benefit from the precise, standard-based construction of measurable claim terms, reducing uncertainty in ANDA litigation and facilitating entry of generic products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower claim scope when patents include measurable parameters like pH, potentially limiting their ability to enforce patents against generics that achieve similar results through different conditions.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents are invalid for omitting a coinventor who cannot be located, and whether 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) provides a mechanism for judicial correction of inventorship when the omitted inventor is unreachable.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that patents naming only U.S.-based inventors were invalid for omitting a Chinese coinventor who could not be located after leaving his employer. The court upheld the denial of judicial inventorship correction under § 256(b), leaving the patents invalid. The decision underscores the critical importance of properly identifying and maintaining contact with all coinventors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from strict enforcement of inventorship requirements, providing a powerful invalidity defense when patent owners fail to name all contributors to the invention.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with overseas manufacturers or contractors face significant patent validity risk if coinventors cannot be located for correction, potentially invalidating entire patent portfolios based on inventorship defects.
